procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders of the courts below annulling the usufructuary mortgage bond in question
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court dealt with the appeal, noting that the Government Advocate conceded the committing court had not complied with certain provisions, but argued the omission was insufficient to overturn the conviction.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court heard the appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 48 of 1957) and allowed the appeal, setting aside the orders of the courts below and holding the transaction binding on the estate of the insolvents.

directions: The orders of the courts below annulling the usufructuary mortgage bond in question are set aside.
The transaction is held binding on the estate of the insolvents.
The lease back to the mortgagors being a part of the same transaction is equally binding on the estate of the insolvents.
The appellant is entitled to his costs throughout, to come out of the estate in the hands of the Official Receiver who must pay his own costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the failure to furnish the accused with copies of documents as required by Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is an illegality that vitiates the trial, or an irregularity curable under Section 537 of the Code.

facts: The accused was convicted of murder and sentenced to death.
The Police Officer and the inquiring Magistrate failed to furnish the accused with copies of necessary documents as required by Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The accused did receive the copies in the Sessions Court before the prosecution witnesses' statements were recorded.
The accused did not complain at the time that the delay in receiving the documents was prejudicial or ask for an adjournment.
The appellant's counsel argued that this failure was an illegality that automatically vitiated the entire trial, regardless of whether any prejudice was caused.
law: The issue hinges on whether the word 'shall' in Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) is mandatory (meaning non-compliance is a fatal illegality) or directory (meaning non-compliance is an irregularity).
Section 537 of the Code allows for an irregularity to be cured if it has not caused prejudice to the accused or resulted in a failure of justice.

The Court referenced the precedent in *Pulukuri Kotayya v. King-Emperor*, which distinguished between a trial conducted in a manner fundamentally different from the Code (an illegality) and an irregularity that occurs during a trial conducted substantially in the prescribed manner (a curable irregularity).
application: The Court held that the word 'shall' in the relevant sections is directory, not mandatory.

The reasoning was that treating the omission as a fatal illegality would have the far-reaching effect of reopening long-concluded trials, which would be contrary to the goal of expeditious justice and the simplifying purpose of the 1955 amendment to the Code.

Applying the principle from *Pulukuri Kotayya*, the Court classified the failure to provide documents as an irregularity that occurred during the course of the proceedings, not a fundamental flaw in the manner of the trial itself.
Because the failure was deemed an irregularity, it could be cured under Section 537 if no prejudice was shown.

The Court found that the accused had failed to show any prejudice. The High Court had noted that the copies were supplied before witness testimony, and the accused made no grievance at the time. Before the Supreme Court, the appellant's counsel made no attempt to argue that prejudice had occurred.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the failure to furnish the accused with copies of documents as required by Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) is not an illegality that automatically vitiates the trial. Instead, it is a curable irregularity under Section 537 of the Code. The proceedings are only invalidated if the accused can show that the omission caused prejudice to their defense.

issue.issue_text: Whether the provisions of Section 173(4) and Section 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure are mandatory or merely directory in nature.

facts: The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death.

During the preliminary inquiry, the police officer and the committing magistrate failed to furnish the appellant with all the necessary documents as required by Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The appellant did not raise this issue during the inquiry or the trial; it was raised for the first time on appeal to the High Court.

The High Court found that the accused had received the necessary copies in the Sessions Court before the witnesses were examined and had not shown any prejudice from the initial failure to provide them.
Before the Supreme Court, the appellant argued that the failure to provide the documents automatically rendered the entire trial null and void, regardless of whether it caused any prejudice.
law: Section 173(4) and Section 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure use the word "shall" in describing the duty of the police and the magistrate to furnish the accused with copies of documents the prosecution intends to rely on.

The interpretation of the word "shall" in a statute can be either mandatory (meaning strict compliance is required, and failure to comply invalidates the action) or directory (meaning non-compliance is an irregularity that does not automatically invalidate the action).
Section 537 of the Code states that a finding, sentence, or order shall not be reversed on account of any error, omission, or irregularity unless a failure of justice has been occasioned.
application: The Court acknowledged that the purpose of these provisions is to safeguard the interests of the accused by ensuring they have all the necessary information to conduct their defense.

However, the Court reasoned that treating these provisions as mandatory would have the "far-reaching effect" of rendering entire proceedings and trials "wholly ineffective." This would lead to reopening long-concluded cases, which would not be conducive to expeditious justice.
Based on this reasoning, the Court held that the word "shall" in both sections is not mandatory but only directory.

The Court established that non-compliance with these provisions is an irregularity that does not invalidate the proceedings unless the accused can show that the omission caused prejudice to their defense.
If no prejudice is shown, the omission is considered a mere irregularity that is curable under Section 537 of the Code.

In this specific case, the appellant made no attempt to demonstrate any prejudice. The documents were eventually supplied, and no grievance was raised at the trial stage about having insufficient time to prepare.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the provisions of Section 173(4) and Section 207A(3) are directory, not mandatory. Therefore, a failure to comply with them does not automatically vitiate the trial. The proceedings are only invalidated if the accused can show that the omission caused prejudice to their defense. Since no prejudice was shown in this case, the non-compliance was a curable irregularity, and the court rejected the argument.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the failure to furnish the accused with copies of documents as required by Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is an illegality that vitiates the trial, or an irregularity curable under Section 537 of the Code.
appellant_arguments: The failure to furnish the required copies is an illegality that vitiates the entire proceedings and the trial.
The omission renders the proceedings null and void, which ipso facto necessitates a fresh trial.
The court should not consider the question of whether the accused was prejudiced by the omission.
respondent_arguments: The failure to furnish copies is not an illegality sufficient to vitiate the trial.
It is an irregularity that is curable under Section 537 of the Code.
The trial is only vitiated if the accused can demonstrate that they were prejudiced in their defense by the omission.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the provisions of Section 173(4) and Section 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure are mandatory or merely directory in nature.
appellant_arguments: The provisions are mandatory, and it is the duty of the magistrate to ensure they are fully complied with.
The use of the word 'shall' in the sections indicates their mandatory nature.
Non-compliance should result in the proceedings being rendered null and void.
respondent_arguments: The provisions are directory, not mandatory.
An omission by a police officer should not have the far-reaching effect of rendering the entire trial ineffective, which would be the result if the provisions were treated as mandatory.
Treating the provisions as mandatory would lead to re-opening concluded trials, which is not conducive to expeditious justice.

cases.principle: Non-compliance with the provisions of Section 360 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was a mere irregularity which could be cured by the provisions of Section 537.

cases.case_name: Pulukuri Kotayya and others v. King-Emperor
cases.principle: The breach of a statutory provision (in that case, Section 162 of the Code) does not necessarily vitiate the proceedings if no prejudice is caused to the accused.

cases.case_name: Gurbachan Singh v. The State of Punjab
cases.principle: To support the view that non-compliance with the procedural provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a curable irregularity if no prejudice is caused to the accused.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Non-compliance with the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which require furnishing documents to the accused, does not automatically vitiate the proceedings. The word 'shall' in these provisions is directory, not mandatory. Such an omission is a curable irregularity under section 537 of the Code, unless it is shown that the accused has been prejudiced in their defense.
obiter: Magistrates have a duty to be circumspect and ensure that accused persons are not handicapped by the failure of police officers to supply necessary copies of documents.
If prejudice to the accused is demonstrated as a result of the omission, the court may re-open the proceedings to insist upon full compliance with the Code.
The distinction between an illegality and an irregularity is one of degree rather than of kind.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The failure to furnish an accused with copies of documents as required by Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not a fatal illegality but a curable irregularity. The provisions are directory, not mandatory, and non-compliance does not automatically vitiate the proceedings unless the accused can demonstrate that the omission caused them actual prejudice in their defense. In the absence of such prejudice, the defect is cured by Section 537 of the Code.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the omission to furnish documents caused prejudice to the accused in their defense, which is the test for determining if an irregularity is curable under Section 537 of the Code.
Whether a statutory provision using the word 'shall' is mandatory or directory, determined by examining the consequences of non-compliance and the overall legislative intent.
why_appellant_lost: The court held that the word 'shall' in Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) is 'not mandatory but only directory,' rejecting the appellant's argument that its use implies an absolute duty that nullifies the proceedings upon breach.

The court rejected the argument that non-compliance is an illegality that ipso facto vitiates the trial, stating, 'we are not prepared to hold that non-compliance with those provisions has, necessarily, the result of vitiating those proceedings and subsequent trial.'

The appellant failed to demonstrate any prejudice, which the court found essential for the omission to have any effect. The court noted, 'It has not been argued, and there is no scope for the argument,that the accused persons have been prejudiced :in any way in their defence.'
The court found that the appellant had raised the grievance for the first time on appeal, not before the Magistrate or the Sessions Judge, which weakened the claim of prejudice.
why_respondent_won: The court agreed that the omission was an irregularity curable under Section 537 of the Code, concluding that 'the irregularity is curable by reference to s. 537 of the Code, as no case of prejudice has been made out.'

The court adopted the respondent's reasoning that the trial is only vitiated if prejudice is shown, stating, 'if it is shown, in a particular case, on behalf of the accused persons that the omission... has caused prejudice to the accused, in the interest of justice, the court may re-open the proceedings'.

The court accepted the argument that treating the provisions as mandatory would have disproportionate consequences, reasoning that 'an omission by a police officer, to fully comply with the provisions of s. 173, should not be allowed to have such a far-reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective.'
policy_considerations: Treating the provisions as mandatory would undermine the goal of simplifying criminal procedure, as it 'will, necessarily, result in re-opening the proceedings and trials which may have been concluded long ago.'
Such a result would be 'neither conducive to expeditious justice nor in the interest of accused persons themselves.'

The court reasoned that a mere omission by a police officer should not be allowed to have the 'far-reaching effect' of rendering an entire trial ineffective, which would be a disproportionate outcome.
